def: The number of a memory location. Every variable is stored at an address; & gives it, as in &x.
A variable that holds an address. int * p = &x; makes p point to x, and *p is the int it points to.
Following a pointer to the value it points to: *p. On a struct pointer, p->data is short for (*p).data.
A pointer value meaning 'points to nothing'. The last node of a list has next == NULL, and an empty tree's root is NULL. Following a NULL pointer crashes the program.
p->field follows the pointer p and picks a field of the struct it points to. Use . on a struct variable and -> on a struct pointer.
Creates a variable on the heap while the program runs and returns its address. It lives until it is deleted.
Frees memory that was made with new. Use delete [] for an array made with new [].
The part of memory where new puts variables. They outlive the function that made them. (Not the same thing as the heap data structure.)
The part of memory where each function call keeps its parameters and local variables. They disappear when the call returns.
A pointer to memory that no longer belongs to the program: after delete, or the address of a local variable whose function has returned.
section: 3. Using memory after delete (a dangling pointer)

def: Memory made with new that can no longer be reached because the last pointer to it was lost, so it can never be deleted.
section: 5. Losing the only pointer (a memory leak)

def: A parameter that is another name for the caller's variable, so changing it changes the caller's variable. Without &, the function gets a copy.
A type that groups several fields under one name, like struct Node { int data; Node * next; };
Adding to a pointer moves it by whole elements: if p points to A[1], then p + 2 points to A[3].
One element of a linked list: a struct holding data and next, a pointer to the following node.
The pointer to the first node of a linked list. An empty list has top == NULL.
The course's function that makes a new node with new, sets its data and sets next to NULL.
A chain of nodes joined by next pointers, starting at top and ending at a node whose next is NULL. It can grow and shrink while the program runs.
Visiting every node: start with curr = top and repeat curr = curr->next until curr is NULL.
Puts a new node in front of the first node and returns it as the new top. O(1).
Walks to the last node and links the new node after it. O(n) without a tail pointer.
Inserts a value into a sorted list at the place that keeps it sorted.
Removes the first node: move top to the second node, then delete the old first node.
Returns the last node of a list: the one whose next is NULL. A loop that runs until the pointer itself is NULL goes one node too far.
section: getLast: stopping at the last node

def: A function that calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem.
The case a recursive function answers without calling itself, such as an empty list or n == 0. Every recursion must reach one.
section: Writing a recursive function: three questions

def: The case where the function calls itself on a smaller problem (for a list: the tail, top->next) and uses the answer.
section: Writing a recursive function: three questions

def: A drawing with one box per call, each call's boxes for the calls it makes below it, used in the lectures to trace recursion.
A collection where the last value in is the first out (LIFO). push adds at the top; pop removes from the top.
A collection where the first value in is the first out (FIFO). enqueue adds at the tail; dequeue removes from the head.
Last in, first out: how a stack behaves.
First in, first out: how a queue behaves.
Data arranged in a hierarchy: one root at the top, and each node may have nodes below it (its children).
The only node of a tree with no parent: the top.
A node with no children (degree 0).
A nonterminal node: one with at least one child.
The number of children a node has.
Nodes with the same parent.
The number of nodes in a tree.
The number of leaves in a tree.
The number of edges from the root to a node. The root is at level 0.
The number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf. A root on its own has height 0; the empty tree has height −1.
A tree that is either empty, or a root with a left subtree and a right subtree, each of which is a binary tree.
The course's binary tree node: data, left and right (and later parent).
Visit the node, then its left subtree, then its right subtree.
Visit the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. On a BST this lists the keys in ascending order.
Visit the left subtree, then the right subtree, then the node.
Visit the nodes level by level, left to right, using a queue.
Every non-leaf node has two non-empty subtrees, and all leaves are at the same level.
All levels except possibly the lowest are completely filled, and the nodes on the lowest level are as far left as possible.
Every non-leaf node has exactly two non-empty subtrees: no node has only one child.
A binary tree where every key in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node's key, and every key in its right subtree is larger.
Starts at the root and goes left for a smaller key, right for a larger one, until it reaches NULL; the new key becomes a leaf there.
Searches a BST by going left or right at each node, so it follows one path down: O(h).
section: containsBST: search that returns the node

def: The next key in inorder. If the node has a right subtree, it is the smallest key there; otherwise go up until you come from a left child.
The previous key in inorder: the mirror image of the successor.
section: The predecessor is the mirror image

def: A third pointer in BTNode that points back up to the node's parent (NULL for the root).
A BST in which every node has at most one child, like a linked list. Inserting keys in sorted order makes one. Its height is n − 1.
section: The worst shape: a degenerate BST

def: The node is a leaf: set its parent's pointer to it to NULL and delete it.
The node has one subtree: connect that subtree to the node's parent in its place. 2(a) no left subtree, 2(b) no right subtree.
The node has two subtrees: copy its inorder successor's key into it, then remove the successor (which has no left subtree).
An almost complete binary tree stored in an array from index 1, where every parent is at least as large as its children (max-heap) or no larger (min-heap).
A heap in which every node is at least as large as its children, so the largest value is at A[1].
A heap in which every node is no larger than its children, so the smallest value is at A[1].
For index i: parent i / 2, left child 2i, right child 2i + 1. Indexes 1 to n / 2 have children; the rest are leaves.
Fixes index i when its subtrees are already heaps: swap A[i] with its larger child, and repeat from there until it is larger than both children. O(log n).
section: maxHeapify: sinking a value into place

def: Turns any array into a max-heap by calling maxHeapify for i from n / 2 down to 1. O(n).
section: buildMaxHeap: making a heap from any array

def: Removes and returns A[1]: move the last value to A[1], shrink the heap, then maxHeapify(1). O(log n).
Puts the new value at the end, then swaps it with its parent while it is larger. O(log n).
Changes A[i] to a larger key, then moves it up like insert.
Build a max-heap, then repeatedly swap the root with the last heap value, shrink the heap and maxHeapify(1). O(n log n) in every case.
A queue that always gives back the highest-priority value next. A max-heap makes a max-priority queue.
Storing each key at a location computed from the key itself, so it can be found again in about constant time.
Turns a key into a location in the table. The course uses h(key) = key % N + 1, giving locations 1 to N.
The array that hashing stores keys in.
When a key hashes to a location that is already full.
After a collision, try the next location (+1), wrapping from N back to 1.
After the x-th collision, move forward x + x² locations (2, 6, 12, ...) from where the collision happened.
Linear probing with a step that depends on the key: k = key % (N − 2) + 1.
Long runs of full locations that build up with linear probing; every key landing in one has to walk to its end.
section: The trouble with linear probing: clusters

def: Each location holds a linked list of all the keys that hash there; a new key goes at the top of its list.
In a probing table, a deleted key's location is set to −1, not to empty, so that searches for keys that collided there keep going.
A pair (V, E): a set of vertices and a set of edges, each edge joining two vertices.
One of the points of a graph (also called a node).
A connection between two vertices. In a directed graph it goes one way, from u to v.
A graph whose edges have a direction, drawn as arrows.
A graph in which every edge carries a number: a distance, cost or time.
In a directed graph: the number of edges entering a vertex, and the number leaving it. Their sum is the degree.
The number of edges on a path.
A directed graph with a path between any two vertices, in both directions.
A V × V table: row u, column v holds 1 (or the weight) if there is an edge from u to v.
For each vertex, a linked list of the vertices its edges lead to.
Visits a vertex, then all its neighbours, then theirs, using a queue: closest vertices first.
Goes as deep as possible along each edge before backing up, using recursion.
The colours BFS and DFS give vertices: WHITE not yet discovered, GREY discovered, BLACK finished.
Finds the cheapest path from a source to every vertex: repeatedly take the lowest-cost vertex off the queue and lower its neighbours' costs where possible. Weights must not be negative.
A set of n − 1 edges that connects every vertex of a connected, undirected, weighted graph with no cycles and the smallest total weight.
section: What is a minimum-cost spanning tree?

def: Sort the edges by weight; add each edge whose two ends are in different trees, and skip the ones that would make a cycle.
Grow one tree from a start vertex: always add the cheapest edge from a used vertex to an unused one.
Pass i finds the smallest value in A[i..n−1] and swaps it into A[i]. O(n²) always.
Each pass swaps neighbouring values that are out of order, so the largest remaining value bubbles to the end. O(n²).
Takes each value in turn and slides it left into its place in the sorted part. O(n²), but O(n) on sorted input.
Sort the left half, sort the right half, merge them. O(n log n) in every case, with extra memory for merging.
Split a problem into smaller parts, solve each part (often recursively), then combine the answers.
partition around a pivot, then quick sort each side. O(n log n) on average, O(n²) in the worst case.
Rearranges A[p..r] around the pivot x = A[r]: values ≤ x end up to its left, larger values to its right, and the pivot lands in its final place.
The value partition compares everything with; the lecture's version uses the last value, A[r].
Sorting inside the original array without a second array. Every sort in the course is in place except merge sort.
section: Why O(n log n), in every case

def: How the number of steps grows with the input size n, keeping only the fastest-growing part and ignoring constant factors.
The same number of steps whatever n is, like insertAtHead or reading A[i].
The number of times n can be halved before reaching 1: about 10 for 1 000. Algorithms that discard half of what is left each step are O(log n).
n steps on each of log n levels: merge sort and heap sort.
Quadratic: a loop inside a loop over n items. Doubling n multiplies the work by 4.
The input that makes an operation take the longest. Exam questions ask for the worst case unless they say otherwise.
